# XrSetup

**Class** · namespace `VRFramework.Core.Editors.Setup` · assembly `VRFramework.Core.Editors` · [view source](https://git.cie-group.cz/vr-framework/vrf4/core/-/blob/interaction/physics-hold/Editor/Setup/XrSetup.cs#L27)

Turns a project into an OpenXR one: XR Plug-in Management configured for both platforms, the
OpenXR loader assigned, the Meta feature set on, and the features the framework's hands and
interactions rely on enabled.
Written to be re-runnable. The previous version deleted everything under Assets/XR and built
it again from scratch, which churned asset GUIDs and left XR Plug-in Management pointing at
assets that no longer existed. Nothing here deletes; it fills in what is missing.

## Methods

### ApplyOpenXrValidationFixes(BuildTargetGroup) {#applyopenxrvalidationfixes-buildtargetgroup}

Applies the automatic fixes for one platform and reports what is left, returning how many
issues still need a person.
Deliberately not part of [`PackageSetup`](/api/vrframework-core-editors-setup/PackageSetup)'s sequence. Most validation rules have
no automatic fix at all, and running the handful that do in the middle of a setup has taken
the editor down often enough that the whole pass was dropped from it. What is left is the
Meta/Pico switch, where the settings really did just change under the project's feet.
This reads OpenXR's own public validation list rather than the wider XR Plug-in Management
one, which is only reachable through an internal method. In exchange for staying on
supported API it does not see the checks the XR samples add - those stay in Project
Settings > XR Plug-in Management > Project Validation, behind the Fix All button.

```csharp

```

### ConfigureOpenXrFeatures() {#configureopenxrfeatures}

Enables Unity's Meta feature set, which is what pulls in the Quest specific OpenXR
features, then turns on the individual features the framework uses and sets the render
mode per platform.
